*Rewritten on 2026-10-15 with AI assistance (Claude), at the maintainer's request, as a general note for any
sea-going trip. The parts specific to the Icelandic logbooks moved to [The Icelandic logbooks in the
grammar](grammar_logbooks.qmd). The port-call term and the name mapping were added with AI assistance (Claude) on
2026-10-19 (decision 147). The parts of "Resolution and provenance" on field groups, moving a value between units,
values known in part, the coarser unit, layer and coverage, and the section "Names under review", were drafted with
AI assistance (Claude) on 2026-10-22 at the maintainer's request. The maintainer chose the word "split"; the rest has
not yet been reviewed (TODO 127). Decisions recorded here are the maintainer's.*

A vessel leaves port, does things at sea, and comes back. A trawler tows its gear, a longliner sets and hauls, a
research vessel trawls and lowers a CTD at survey stations, an oceanographic cruise samples plankton along a section,
and a ship of opportunity logs the sea surface as it passes. Each of these is recorded by its own system, with its own
names (`visir`, `station_id`, `StNo`, `haul_id`), its own encodings (degrees and minutes, decimal degrees, statistical
rectangles) and its own resolution: one row per operation in one system, one row per day and rectangle in another.

This note proposes one way to represent all of them: a small set of tables, keys and column names that any such
record can be mapped onto. It is a grammar of data *representation*, the layer below a grammar of data manipulation
[@wickham2010] and of data analysis [@yang2025]: an analysis can only compute metrics over dimensions once the
dimensions mean the same thing in every source.

# The structure

## Four levels and the streams beside them

```
Trip                          a voyage: from port, at sea, back to port
 └── Station                  where and when the vessel stopped to do something
      └── Sample              one act done there (a tow, a set, a cast, a net haul, a watch)
           └── Observation    what that act recorded (catch by species, a fish, a depth bin)

beside the hierarchy, keyed on vessel and time:
     the track                positions along the whole trip (AIS, VMS, GPS loggers)
     underway sensors         continuous recordings (surface temperature, echograms)
     declarations ashore      what was reported after the trip (landings)
```

Each level is one-to-many to the next, and keys run downward only: a child carries its parent's key.

- A **trip** may have no stations (turned back, steamed between ports).
- A **station** is any stop or interval at which the vessel does something other than transit: a fishing operation, a
  survey haul, a CTD cast, an acoustic transect, a visual watch.
- A **sample** is one act at a station. A research station can hold a trawl haul and a CTD cast, two samples sharing
  the station's time and place. A commercial station usually holds one fishing sample, and the two levels are stored as
  one row (the *collapsed* case, @sec-sample).
- An **observation** is one value or row produced by a sample: a species' catch, one fish's length, one depth bin of a
  profile, one sighting.

The **streams** are not levels. They are recorded continuously, with no deployment and no retrieval, and they are
joined to the hierarchy afterwards by vessel and time (`vid`, `time` between a trip's or a sample's bounds), never by
a shared key.

## Two questions that place every field {#sec-field-groups}

Every field in a sea-going record answers two questions: **what does it describe**, and **when is it known**. The
answers give the field groups:

| Field group | Describes | Known | Examples |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Identification** | the record | — | vessel, trip and station numbers, survey, country |
| **Design** | the station | before | survey and stratum, protocol, the planned operation, what the catch is processed as (DATRAS `DataType`); for commercial fishing, the target or licence where recorded |
| **Temporal envelope** | the station | after | start and end of the time the vessel was occupied |
| **Spatial envelope** | the station | after | positions at start and end, statistical rectangle |
| **Configuration** | the sample | before | how the gear or instrument is set up: mesh, door weight, headline and sweep length, number of hooks or nets, a CTD's sensor suite, a plankton net's mouth area |
| **In-situ measurement** | the sample | during | what the deployed gear or instrument itself measured: door spread, wing spread, net opening, flowmeter counts |
| **Execution** | the sample | during | how the vessel worked it: speed over ground, course, distance, warp out, the depth the gear worked at |
| **Environment** | the sea | during | the state of the sea and air, whether or not anything was deployed: water depth, temperatures, salinity, wind, sea state, currents, ice |
| **Outcome** | the sample | after | valid or not, why disrupted, gear lost, record edited |
| **Observation** | the sample's product | after | catch, individuals, profile bins, counts |

### The rule that matters most: the operation or the sea

A value describes either **the operation** (configuration, in-situ, execution, outcome) or **the sea** (environment).
The test is whether it would exist if nothing had been deployed. The sea has a depth, a temperature and a wind with or
without a net in it, but a net has a fishing depth only while it fishes.

**Depth is the case that most often goes wrong.** Two different variables share one word:

- **water depth** (`z1`, `z2`): the depth of the sea at the station, an environmental value. It can be measured by the
  echosounder at any time, or read from a bathymetry;
- **gear depth** (`z1_gear`, `z2_gear`): the depth at which the gear or instrument worked, an execution value. A
  pelagic trawl at 300 m in 1,000 m of water has a gear depth of 300 and a water depth of 1,000.

For gear on the bottom the two coincide, which is why many systems record only one "depth". A source that does not
say which it is should not be guessed into one:
- **bottom-contact gear:** keep the value as water depth;
- **pelagic gear:** keep it as recorded, with its kind marked unknown.

The same rule separates a headline temperature measured by a sensor on the trawl, which is environment at the gear's
depth, from the headline's height, which is in-situ geometry.

### A worked example: DATRAS HH

The ICES DATRAS haul header (HH) is a rich, well-documented station record. It is one wide row per haul, and it holds
nearly every field group:

| Field group | HH columns |
|---|---|
| Identification | Survey, Quarter, Country, Ship, StNo, HaulNo, Year |
| Design | DataType, StdSpecRecCode, BySpecRecCode, Stratum, PelSampType |
| Temporal envelope | Year, Month, Day, TimeShot, HaulDur, DayNight |
| Spatial envelope | ShootLat, ShootLong, HaulLat, HaulLong, StatRec |
| Configuration | Gear, GearExp, DoorType, DoorWgt, DoorSurface, SweepLngt, Warplngt, Warpdia, Rigging, Tickler, Buoyancy, KiteDim, WgtGroundRope, CodendMesh |
| In-situ measurement | Netopening, DoorSpread, WingSpread |
| Execution | Distance, TowDir, GroundSpeed, SpeedWater, MinTrawlDepth, MaxTrawlDepth |
| Environment | Depth, SurTemp, BotTemp, SurSal, BotSal, WindDir, WindSpeed, SwellDir, SwellHeight, SurCurDir, SurCurSpeed, BotCurDir, BotCurSpeed, ThermoCline, ThClineDepth, SecchiDepth, Turbidity, TidePhase, TideSpeed |
| Outcome | HaulVal |

HH can be one wide row because it describes **one class of gear**: every haul is a towed trawl, so every column
applies. A source that covers many gears (longlines, gillnets, trawls, dredges, traps, seines) cannot do that without
mostly empty columns whose meaning changes with the gear. The grammar keeps HH's grouping, and changes the layout only
where gears differ: the configuration (@sec-configuration).

# The levels

## Trip

A voyage from a port and back: a fishing trip, a survey leg, a cruise. For commercial vessels it is also an
administrative unit (a landing declaration, a licence period).

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `.tid` | int / chr | trip key |
| `vid` | int / chr | vessel |
| `T1`, `T2` | datetime | departure, return (landing) |
| `hid1`, `hid2` | int / chr | departure and return port, in the source's own code |
| `pid1`, `pid2` | chr | the same ports in the standard port key |
| `n_crew` | int | crew |
| `source` | chr | the system or app that recorded the trip |

Some systems record no trip, and it is derived: the stations of one vessel that share a landing date and port, or the
rows of an EU logbook that share departure and landing times. A declared date is what was declared; the times a vessel
actually left and returned come from the track (@sec-streams).

## Station

The envelope of what happened at one place and time: where and when the vessel was occupied, not what it did.

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `.sid` | int / chr | station key |
| `.tid` | | the trip |
| `date` | date | the administrative date of the station |
| `s1`, `s2` | datetime | outer time bounds: the earliest and latest time of any sample at the station |
| `lon1`, `lat1`, `lon2`, `lat2` | dbl | positions at `s1` and `s2`, decimal degrees |
| `sq`, `ssq` | int / chr | statistical rectangle and sub-rectangle, from the position |
| `station_type` | chr | what the row covers (@sec-resolution) |

`s1`/`s2` and the positions are *derived* bounds: with one sample, `s1` is that sample's first time and `s2` its last.
They become independent the moment a station holds two samples with their own times. The positions are time-ordered
(start, end) rather than minimum and maximum, so the direction of a tow is kept.

## Sample {#sec-sample}

One act at a station, with its own instrument, method and times.

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `.smid` | int / chr | sample key (needed once a station holds more than one sample) |
| `.sid` | | the station |
| `sample_type` | chr | `fishing`, `ctd`, `plankton`, `acoustic`, `visual`, `logger`, … |
| `t1`, `t2`, `t3`, `t4` | datetime | the four events of the act (below) |

**The collapsed case.** In commercial logbooks a station holds exactly one fishing sample, so the sample has no table
of its own: its columns sit beside the station's, keyed on `.sid`, and `.smid` is not needed. They are still sample
attributes, and code should treat them as such.

### Four events

Any deployment goes through four events: going in, reaching working position, leaving it, and coming out. The grammar
names them `t1` to `t4` in the order they happen. Few systems record all four:

| Event | Mobile gear (trawl, dredge, seine) | Static gear (longline, gillnet, trap) | CTD cast | Plankton net | Acoustic transect | Visual watch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `t1` | gear enters the water | first buoy in | in the water | in the water | — | watch begins |
| `t2` | on the bottom (or at depth): fishing starts | last buoy in: soak starts | at maximum depth | at depth, net opens | transect starts | — |
| `t3` | off the bottom: fishing ends | first buoy out: hauling starts | ascent begins | net closes, retrieval | transect ends | — |
| `t4` | gear out of the water | last buoy out | on deck | on deck | — | watch ends |

From the events:

- **The active interval** is `[t2, t3]`. For a trawl it is the tow; for static gear, the soak.
- **The location window** `[w1, w2]` is where the vessel's own position tells where the gear was:
  - for mobile gear `[t2, t3]`, since the vessel tows the gear;
  - for static gear `[t3, t4]`, since the vessel is over the gear only while hauling;
  - joining the track on `[w1, w2]` then needs no rule per gear.
- **Overlaps.** Within one vessel, deployment windows `[t1, t2]` cannot overlap, and neither can hauling windows
  `[t3, t4]`. Outer windows `[t1, t4]` can: a longliner sets a new line while an earlier one soaks.

### The fishing sample

A fishing sample adds the gear and the effort to `t1`-`t4`:

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `gid` | int / chr | gear code |
| `gear` | chr | gear class (ICES ISSCFG / métier codes: `OTB`, `LLS`, `GNS`, …) |
| `duration_m` | dbl | the active interval, minutes |
| `effort_count` | dbl | what fishes at once: hooks, nets, jigs, traps; 1 for a single towed gear |
| `effort_duration` | dbl | the duration in the unit of `effort_unit` |
| `effort_unit` | chr | `gear-minutes`, `hook-days`, `net-days`, `jig-hours`, `trap-hours`, `setting` |
| `effort` | dbl | `effort_count × effort_duration` |
| `w1`, `w2` | datetime | the location window |
| `z1_gear`, `z2_gear` | dbl | the depth the gear worked at, m (execution) |
| `n_lost` | int | gear lost (outcome) |

Other sample types have their own measure of effort: volume filtered for a plankton net, distance sailed for an
acoustic transect, time watched for a visual watch.

## Configuration: one row per part, one column per measure {#sec-configuration}

How a gear or instrument is set up is the field group that differs most between gears. A trawl has doors, sweeps, a
headline and a codend. A gillnet fleet has a number of nets, their length, their height and their mesh. A longline has
hooks and tubs, and a dredge has a width and a weight. One wide table across all of them, as HH is for trawls alone,
would hold mostly empty columns, and a column such as "width" or "length" would change meaning from gear to gear.

The grammar instead **harmonises by measure**:

- **Rows:** a configuration row is one *part* of the gear at one sample (codend, net, hook, door, sweep, headline,
  dredge, trap, seine, grid, square window).
- **Columns:** one column per *measure*, the same column for the same measure whatever the part or the gear. A mesh
  size is a mesh size on a codend, a gillnet or a seine, and a count is a count of nets, hooks, traps or trawls.

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `.sid` (or `.smid`) | | the sample |
| `part` | chr | `gear`, `codend`, `net`, `hook`, `line`, `jig`, `trap`, `door`, `sweep`, `headline`, `footrope`, `rope`, `dredge`, `seine`, `grid`, `square_window`, … |
| `n` | dbl | how many of the part |
| `length_m`, `width_m`, `height_m` | dbl | dimensions, metres |
| `height_meshes` | dbl | height counted in meshes |
| `weight_kg`, `area_m2` | dbl | weight, area |
| `mesh_size_mm` | dbl | mesh size, millimetres |
| `mesh_orientation` | chr | `T0`, `T45`, `T90` |
| `meshes_around` | dbl | circumference in meshes |
| `type` | chr | the source's own type code or name (grid type, dredge type) |
| `material` | chr | as recorded |
| `present` | lgl | for a part that is either fitted or not |

A part with no recorded measure has no row. A trawl haul becomes five or six rows (gear, codend, doors, sweeps,
headline), and a gillnet set one or two (net, gear). The count that is `effort_count` on the sample is the `n` of the
gear's working part (nets, hooks, traps, jigs). For an instrument the same shape serves: part `sensor`, `type` the
sensor, `n` its count.

## Environment

The state of the sea and air at the station, recorded whether or not anything was deployed: one row per station. A
variable read at both ends of the station takes the numeric suffix (1 at the start, 2 at the end), as positions do.

| Column | Unit | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `z1`, `z2` | m | water depth |
| `temp1_surface`, `temp2_surface` | °C | sea-surface temperature |
| `temp1_bottom`, `temp2_bottom` | °C | bottom temperature |
| `temp1_headline`, `temp2_headline` | °C | temperature at the gear (a sensor on the trawl's headline) |
| `temp1_air` | °C | air temperature |
| `salinity1_surface`, `salinity1_bottom` | PSU | salinity |
| `wind_direction` | degrees | wind from |
| `wind_force`, `wind_speed` | Beaufort, m/s | wind |
| `sea_state` | code | sea state, in the source's scale |
| `swell_direction`, `swell_height` | degrees, m | swell |
| `current_direction`, `current_speed` | degrees, m/s | current |

A full profile (a CTD cast, a temperature chain) is not a row here but a sample with its own observations, one per
depth bin. A single value at the station is environment, and a sequence is a sample.

## Observation

What a sample produced. Its shape depends on the sample type, and each type has its own table keyed on the sample:

| Sample type | Observation table | One row per |
|---|---|---|
| fishing | `catch` (`.sid`, `sid`, `catch` kg, `condition`) | species and condition |
| fishing, protected species | bycatch counts | taxon |
| survey haul | lengths, individuals (DATRAS HL, CA) | length class, or individual |
| CTD | profile | depth bin |
| logger | readings | time |
| visual | sightings | sighting |

`.sid` (the station) and `sid` (the species) share their letters by accident: the dot marks the synthetic key.

# The streams {#sec-streams}

## The track

Positions recorded continuously through the trip: AIS, VMS, a GPS logger. One row per position (`vid`, `time`, `lon`,
`lat`, `speed`, `heading`, `provider`), no station key. The track is joined to the hierarchy by time:

- to a trip on `[T1, T2]`;
- to a fishing sample on its location window `[w1, w2]`.

Where the logbook has no times, the track can supply them. A station built from the track carries
`station_type = "reconstructed"`, and every value it supplies carries basis `reconstructed`.

The terms used for the track (decision 075; "port call", and the names ramb uses, from decision 147):

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **port** | where a trip starts and ends: a polygon in the port layer. |
| `pid` | port id, the polygon's id (ramb: `port_id`). |
| `hid` | a source's own port code (the logbook's, the landings', a tracking system's). |
| **port call** | an interval a vessel spends in port, from arrival to departure (called a *stay* until decision 147). Its values (`T_in`, `T_out`, duration, `pid`) live once, in the port-call table; a position carries only the port call's key, numbered per vessel by `T_in` (a port call is not cut at New Year). |
| **voyage** | any movement cut from the track, from one port call to the next: fishing trips and everything else. Its key is numbered per vessel and year (a voyage is cut at New Year). The trail repeats a few of its voyage's values on each fix (`gid_voyage`, `s1_voyage`, `s2_voyage`, `gear_voyage_basis`, `.tid_voyage`, `n_tid_voyage`), a deliberate exception to keys only, so the trail can be read alone (decision 147). |
| **trip** | a fishing trip, declared in the logbook (`.tid`, `T1`/`T2`); one voyage or more on which the vessel fishes. |
| **record** | a logbook record at any resolution (a station, a day, a trip). |
| **ping** | one position report; `provider` is the feed it came from. |
| **frozen input** | the output of a one-time fix, built once, reviewed, and read by the build as an input it never rebuilds. |

fishycode's tables and ramb's functions name some of these columns differently. The two keys have followed ramb since
the rebuild of 2026-10-19 (decisions 147 and 149); the rest keep the mapping:

| fishycode | ramb | what |
|---|---|---|
| `port_call_id` (`stay` until decision 149) | `port_call_id` | a port call's key, per vessel |
| `voyage_id` (`voyage` until decision 149) | `voyage_id` | a voyage's key, with `vid` and `year` |
| `pid` | `port_id` | a port |
| `pid1`, `pid2` | `port_from`, `port_to` | a voyage's ports |
| `.tid`, `.sid`, with `schema` | `trip_id`, or the `keys` given | a declared trip or station |
| `T1_ais`, `T2_ais` | `T1_voyage`, `T2_voyage` | a voyage's times beside a trip's |

## Underway sensors

Continuous recordings that span stations (sea-surface temperature and salinity, echograms, a temperature chain) are a
stream keyed on (`vid`, `time`, `instrument_id`). They are attributed to a station only where the time is unambiguous.
A logger on the gear itself, recording only while the gear fishes, is a sample instead (`sample_type = "logger"`), with
its readings as observations.

## Declarations ashore

Landings are a stream made ashore, by a buyer, a harbour or an authority, after the trip. Their natural keys are the
trip's own: vessel, landing date, port.

```
Trip  ──(vid, T2, hid2)──→  Landing (.lid)
 └── Station
      └── Catch       ←──── should sum to ────→  landed catch by species
```

| Column | Type | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `.lid` | int / chr | landing key |
| `vid` | | vessel |
| `T2` | datetime | landing date |
| `hid2` | | landing port |
| `sid` | | species |
| `catch` | dbl | landed weight, kg |

Raw landing records are often finer than a trip (one row per delivery, buyer or species). They are collapsed to one
landing per vessel, date and port before they are matched. The match between a landing (`.lid`) and a trip (`.tid`) is
an inference, stored as a crosswalk table holding both keys, never a shared key.

The difference between logged and landed catch is information, not error. The logbook is the skipper's estimate at
sea, and the landing is weighed. Keeping the two streams apart is what makes the difference measurable.

# Resolution and provenance

Four questions place a value:

- **what it covers**: its resolution;
- **how it was obtained**: its basis;
- **which source gave it**: its layer;
- **how much of its population that source holds**: its coverage.

The answers change with the period and the place, even within one source. A record office may keep a vessel's month
for decades, then drop the vessel, then record the day. Its neighbour may have kept the day all along. A single
method fits no such history. A cascade does: for each value the best source present answers, the next one where it is
missing, and the value carries which answered ([the one-flow document](one_flow.qmd)). The sections below give the
terms the cascade records.

## What a row covers {#sec-resolution}

Systems resolve the hierarchy to different depths:

| `station_type` | A row is | Typical keys | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| `operation` | one operation | `.sid`, times, positions | electronic logbooks, survey hauls |
| `event` | an aggregate: trip × gear × day × rectangle | trip, gear, date, rectangle | EU eflalo |
| `monthly_aggregate` | an aggregate over a month | year, month, vessel, gear, rectangle | historical logbooks |
| `annual_aggregate` | an aggregate over a year | year, area, species | historical statistics |
| `reconstructed` | a station built from the track | `vid`, time window | AIS or VMS fishing pings |

The station table carries `station_type`, so that any analysis sensitive to the difference (swept area, tow-time
distributions, overlap checks) can filter or weight by it. The WGSFD one-flow document calls the same thing a record's
*resolution*.

Aggregates can be kept two ways:

- **in their own table**, keyed on their grouping, and brought to a common resolution by summarising the stations when
  both are needed (preferred when stations are the main source);
- **as stations**, with a synthetic `.sid` and `.tid`, the rectangle's centre as position and the month's bounds as
  times. This keeps one table, at the cost of a precision that is not there, and it must be flagged.

Aggregates are sometimes stored among real operations in the same table. A free-text comment column is often the only
sign, so it should be read before anything else in a conversion.

## What each field group covers {#sec-resolution-groups}

A row's `station_type` says what the row covers as a whole. Its field groups (@sec-field-groups) can each be resolved
to a different depth. A historical register of weighed landings may know the vessel, the month, the buying station's
port, the gear and the species, but no day and no position. The same office's later tables may drop the vessel for
some years. A modern landing knows the hour. The depth of each group is a property of the source in a period and a
place, not of the source for ever.

| field group | from finest to coarsest |
|---|---|
| identification (the vessel) | a hull (`vid`) · a class or fleet segment · `none` |
| temporal envelope | an instant · a day · a set of days within a period · a month · a year |
| spatial envelope | a position · a rectangle or sub-rectangle · an area · a port · `none` |
| configuration (the gear) | the gear as configured · a gear code · a gear class · `none` |
| observation (the catch) | the sample's, as the row: per operation, day × rectangle, trip, landing, month or year |

Where a source's depth differs between groups, or changes within the source over time, each group carries its own
resolution beside its basis and its layer: `<group>_resolution` (the unit its value was recorded on), `<group>_basis`
and `<group>_layer` (for example `time_resolution`, `place_resolution`). These are three more columns per group on the
same row, not a table of their own. The row stays one observation with one column per variable, as tidy data asks
[@wickham2014]. Provenance is a variable describing how the group was observed. The group names are a proposal, not
yet fixed.

### Moving a value between units {#sec-moving}

A value recorded on one unit is often needed on another:
- a trip's gear on each of its fixes;
- a landing's weight on the hauls of its trip;
- the fixes' hours in a grid cell.

How a value moves depends on its kind. The kind is declared once per variable, in the data dictionary:

- **additive**: the parts add up to the whole (a weight, a count, hours, a value in money);
- **non-additive**: a price, a rate, a mean, a density;
- **a label**: a gear, a port, a species.

| moving to | additive | non-additive, or a label |
|---|---|---|
| finer units | **split** by a key: the parts sum to the whole | **inherited**: each part takes the whole's value |
| coarser units | **aggregated**: summed | **aggregated**: a weighted mean, or the most frequent label |
| between observations | — | **interpolated**: estimated from the observations either side |

No column of its own is needed for the move. It follows from three things already there:
- the value's own resolution (`<group>_resolution`);
- the row's resolution;
- the variable's kind.

A value whose own unit is coarser than the row's was split or inherited. One whose unit is finer was aggregated. One
whose unit is the same is as recorded.

**A split needs a key**: what weighs the parts, such as fishing hours, logged weight or equal shares. The key goes in
its own column, `<group>_key`, and the value's basis says whose key it was:

- `derived`: the record's own values;
- `reconstructed`: the same unit's data in another source, for example a landing split over the vessel's own fixes by
  their hours;
- `synthesised`: a rule, or other units' data, for example equal shares, or the hauls that other vessels logged in the
  same month and port.

Raising a sample to a census total is a split, with the sample as the key.

**Down and back up returns the value.**
- The parts of a split aggregate to the total they came from.
- Inherited copies aggregate to the parent's value.

Every step that moves a value can be held to that test. For additive quantities it is the rule that every kilogram
logged or landed is counted once (@sec-coarser-unit). An interpolated value has no such round trip. It passes through
the observations, and its basis is `synthesised`.

### Known in part: bounds and sets {#sec-partial}

Some values are known only in part. Two forms are common:

- **a bound**: the departure was after the last landing and before the first haul. It is two columns (`T1_from`,
  `T1_to`) that close to a point where the evidence allows.
- **a set**: the vessel landed on the 3rd, the 9th and the 22nd of the month, but the month's weight is one total. It
  is a child table with one row per member (unit × day), holding no share of the quantity.

In a set, the weight stays on the parent. A step may split it only by a key (@sec-moving).

Neither form is forced to a point, and neither is dropped: a bound is better than a guessed time, and a set of days is
better than none.

### The coarser unit {#sec-coarser-unit}

Every quantity logged or landed ends on some unit. Where the processing cannot reach the finest unit, the quantity
stays on the finest it can reach, and the row's resolution says which: a vessel-month with no day, a port-month with no
vessel. That is an outcome, not a gap. Its basis is that of its source, and its sum is part of every total. `none` is
for a value no source has. A quantity that a source has is never `none`, however coarse.

Strictly, a landing, a vessel-month and a port-month are three observational units, and tidy data would give each its
own table [@wickham2014]. The grammar allows that (above). Where totals must close (every kilogram in once, every
kilogram out once), it prefers one table with `resolution`, and empty keys where a level is not resolved: a sum over
one table cannot lose a kilogram between two. The departure from strict tidiness is deliberate.

## Basis: where a value came from

Every value the processing infers carries a **basis**:

| basis | the value is |
|---|---|
| `recorded` | as the source recorded it (a unit conversion does not change this) |
| `derived` | computed from recorded values of the same record (`t2` plus a duration) |
| `reconstructed` | from another source (times from the track, depth from a bathymetry) |
| `synthesised` | from a rule or a typical value |
| `none` | no source has it |

Modifiers (such as `capped`) go in their own column. A split value takes the basis of its key (@sec-moving).

**The original is never destroyed.** A correction adds columns, and the source value stays beside the corrected one
(`lon1_raw` beside `lon1`).

## Layer: which source gave it {#sec-layer}

The basis says how a value was obtained. The **layer** says which source gave it: the system, the table and the copy
(a weighing register, an electronic logbook, a dump of a given date). Where several sources hold the same value, the
cascade takes the best one present, and the layer records which answered. Like the basis, it is kept per field group
(`<group>_layer`).

The order of the sources, best first, is declared in a table, per period and field group, not written into code. A
better source found later then changes a row of that table, not the processing.

**Lineage.** Sources are often copies of one another: a national statistic compiled from a register, or a database fed
each night from another. A **witness**, a source read only to check another, confirms a value only if its lineage is
independent of the source it checks. Agreement between two copies of one record shows that the columns mean what they
are read to mean. It does not show that the record is right. A source's lineage, as far as it is known, belongs to its
description.

## Coverage: census or sample {#sec-coverage}

A stream is a **census** where it holds every unit of its population (every landing weighed, every vessel above a size
carrying AIS). It is a **sample** where it holds some: an observer programme, or logbooks kept by some vessels only.

Coverage belongs to a stream in a period and a place, not to the stream for ever. Logbooks that were a sample become a
census once they are mandatory and electronic. Coverage is measured as the share of a census that the sample holds,
counted in units or in weight. It is kept with the stream's description, per period and place, and reaches the rows
through the basis.

Two rules follow:

- **Totals come from a census.** A sample places them (where, when, with what gear), but does not add to them.
- **Where a sample places a census quantity, the quantity is split with the sample as the key.** The basis then says
  whose sample it was (@sec-moving).

## Units

Every measure is metric, and its unit is in the column name where the name alone would not say it (`length_m`,
`weight_kg`, `mesh_size_mm`). A conversion from fathoms, feet or inches is a unit conversion, recorded in the data
dictionary, and the source value stays in the raw dump.

# Names

## The vocabulary

| Name | Level | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `.tid`, `.sid`, `.smid`, `.lid` | trip, station, sample, landing | synthetic keys |
| `vid` | trip | vessel |
| `cid` | trip | country |
| `T1`, `T2` | trip | departure, return |
| `hid1`, `hid2` / `pid1`, `pid2` | trip | ports, source code / standard key |
| `date` | station | administrative date |
| `s1`, `s2` | station | outer time bounds (derived) |
| `lon1`, `lat1`, `lon2`, `lat2` | station | positions at start and end |
| `sq`, `ssq` | station | rectangle, sub-rectangle |
| `station_type` | station | what the row covers |
| `sample_type` | sample | the kind of act |
| `t1`-`t4` | sample | the four events |
| `w1`, `w2` | fishing sample | the location window |
| `gid`, `gear` | fishing sample | gear code, gear class |
| `effort_count`, `effort_duration`, `effort_unit`, `effort` | fishing sample | effort |
| `z1_gear`, `z2_gear` | sample | the depth the gear worked at |
| `part`, `n`, `length_m`, …, `mesh_size_mm` | configuration | @sec-configuration |
| `z1`, `z2`, `temp1_surface`, … | environment | the state of the sea |
| `sid` | observation | species |
| `catch` | observation | weight, kg |
| `schema` | every table | the source system |
| `basis` (and `<column>_basis`) | any | where a value came from |
| `resolution` (and `<group>_resolution`) | any | what a row, or one of its field groups, covers (@sec-resolution-groups) |
| `<group>_layer` | any | which source gave a field group (@sec-layer) |
| `<group>_key` | any | what weighed a split (@sec-moving) |

## The conventions

- **A dot marks a synthetic key** (`.tid`, `.sid`, `.smid`, `.lid`), as against a natural one (`vid`, `sid`). A column
  made inside processing and absent from the raw data carries one too.
- **Time names follow the level:** uppercase `T1`/`T2` for the trip, lowercase `s1`/`s2` for the station, `t1`-`t4`
  for the sample.
- **A numeric suffix is the start (1) or the end (2):** `lon1`/`lon2`, `z1`/`z2`, `temp1_bottom`/`temp2_bottom`. Where
  the measure is qualified, the number follows the measure and the place follows the number.
- **A synthetic key belongs to one system.** `.tid` and `.sid` are the logbook's. Another system with its own trips
  gets its own name (`.lid` for landings), and the link between two systems is a crosswalk of inferred matches, never a
  shared column. Where one table holds records from several systems, its keys are `(key, schema)`: two systems'
  ids are never one value space, whatever their numbers.

## Names under review {#sec-naming-review}

## Review pending (TODO 127)

This section is a proposal. It was drafted with AI assistance (Claude) on 2026-10-22 and has not been reviewed. Only
the word **split** is decided (the maintainer). Every other rule and name below waits for the maintainer, item by
item. Until then the names in use stay as they are, here and in ramb. Some passages of this document use words the
review would change; they are listed under "Clashes".
:::

Names are the hardest thing to change later. This review covers the grammar's nouns and the verbs of the functions
that apply it (ramb), and holds them to one set of rules.

### The rules proposed

1. **One concept, one word; one word, one concept**, across everything a reader sees together: this grammar, the
   one-flow document and ramb.
2. **The part of speech follows the job:**
   - verbs name functions;
   - nouns name tables, columns and levels, and are the values that say *what a thing is* (`operation`, `trip`,
     `month`);
   - past participles are the values that say *how a value came to be* (`recorded`, `split`);
   - adjectives are the values of a property.
3. **One root through its forms.** The verb, the noun and the participle of a concept share a root (to split, a split,
   split; to reconstruct, a reconstruction, reconstructed). A label then names the act that made it.
4. **Acts that mirror each other get words that pair**: keep and drop, encode and decode, split and aggregate, link and
   assign.
5. **A name in use changes only for a strong reason**:
   - a *clash*: one word, two meanings, in front of the same reader;
   - a *synonym*: two words for one concept.
6. **Plain words over jargon**, avoiding words with a strong other meaning in statistics or in fisheries management:
   *allocate* (quota), *distribution* (probability), *transfer* (quota transfer).

Decided already, and kept: a flow step's function takes a **shape verb** that says what comes back. `create` returns a
table of its own, `add` the input with columns added, `flag` a flag column, and `link` a table of pairs (ramb's naming
rule). A tool takes an **act verb**, and the act a step performs is said in its title and in the labels it writes. The
review gives the act verbs a vocabulary.

### The acts

| act | verb | noun | participle | mirror | in use now |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| take data from storage | read | reading | read | write | `rb_read_*` |
| map values through a reference table | look up | lookup | looked up | — | `rb_lookup_mmsi_country` |
| change units of measure | convert | conversion | converted | convert back | `rb_convert_speed` |
| bring codes or forms to a standard | standardise | standardisation | standardised | — | `rb_standardise_gear_meshsize` |
| turn coordinates into a code | encode | encoding | encoded | decode (missing) | `rb_encode_ices_rectangle` |
| take part of a code | extract | extraction | extracted | — | `rb_extract_metier` |
| compute a measure from a row or series | calculate (`calc`) | calculation | → basis `derived` | — | `rb_calc_*` |
| put a value in a class by a rule | classify | classification | classified | — | `rb_classify_mmsi`, `rb_add_fishing` |
| estimate a value from a model | predict | prediction | predicted | — | `rb_predict_gear_width` |
| replace a missing value | fill | filling | filled | — | `rb_fill_gear_width`, `rb_pad_harbour` |
| mark a row with a judgement, keep it | flag | flag | flagged | — | `rb_flag_*` |
| bound a value | cap | cap | capped | — | `rb_cap_*`, `rb_limit_record_duration` |
| keep or drop rows by a condition | keep, drop | — | kept, dropped | each other | `rb_keep_in_polygons`, `rb_drop_in_polygons` |
| test a condition, return yes or no | detect | detection | detected | — | `rb_detect_*`, `rb_check_trip_crosses_year` |
| cut a series into intervals | segment | segment | segmented | — | `rb_create_voyages`, `rb_create_port_calls`, … |
| relate entities, candidates many to many | link | link | linked | assign | `rb_link_*` |
| resolve a link to one | assign | assignment | assigned | link | `rb_add_record`, `rb_add_voyages` |
| an additive total down, by a key | **split** (decided) | split | split | aggregate | `rb_share_catch` |
| a non-additive value or label down, unchanged | inherit | inheritance | inherited | aggregate | the `rb_add_*` that join a parent's columns |
| combine up: sum, weighted mean, mode | aggregate | aggregation | aggregated | split, inherit | `*_aggregate` (@sec-resolution) |
| estimate between observations | interpolate | interpolation | interpolated | thin (missing) | `rb_interpolate*` |
| take the best source present, fall back | cascade | cascade | → `<group>_layer` | — | the design (@sec-layer) |
| make two accounts agree, explain the rest | reconcile | reconciliation | reconciled | — | fishycode's reconciled trips |
| check every record against witnesses | audit | audit | audited | — | fishycode's audits |
| show | plot, peek, summarise | plot, summary | — | — | `rb_plot_*`, `rb_peek`, `rb_summarise_track` |

### Clashes: one word, two meanings

| word | meaning 1 | meaning 2 | proposal |
|---|---|---|---|
| **event** | `station_type = "event"`: an aggregate over trip × gear × day × rectangle | the four events `t1`-`t4` | `daily_aggregate`, beside `monthly_aggregate` and `annual_aggregate` |
| **reconstructed** | `station_type`: a station built from the track | the basis: a value from another source | `reconstruction` (the noun, rule 3), or the station's basis (see `station_type` below) |
| **sample** | the level: one act at a station | coverage: census or sample (@sec-coverage) | coverage values `full` and `partial` |
| **set** | static gear: set and haul | "a set of days" (@sec-partial) | "a list of days" |
| **unit** | the thing a value belongs to (@sec-moving) | units of measure (the section "Units") | that section becomes "Units of measure" |
| **window** | the location window `w1`, `w2` | the time a vessel is busy with a logbook record (ramb's record windows) | "location window" and "record window", each said in full |
| **allocation** | an audit of every link and split the flow makes | quota allocation; in accounting, a whole item to one place | "flow audit", or kept and defined |

### Synonyms: two words, one concept

| words | concept | proposal |
|---|---|---|
| `station_type` / `resolution` | what a row covers (@sec-resolution says they are one) | one column, `resolution`, with one value set (`operation`, `day`, `month`, `year`, `trip`, …); how the station was obtained moves to its basis |
| ping / fix / position | one position report of a vessel | one word |
| track / trail | the positions of a vessel over time | **track** for the positions as received (the stream), **trail** for the track with its labels (the product) |
| record / station, sample | a logbook entry at any resolution | ramb's `record` is this grammar's station with its fishing sample (the collapsed case), said in the name mapping (@sec-streams) |
| assign / add | a flow step that adds columns | the one-flow document's sketch takes ramb's names (`add_*`, `split_catch`) |
| share / split | an additive total down by a key | `split` (decided) |
| check / detect | test a condition | `detect`; `check` only where nothing changes but a warning |
| cap / limit | bound a value | `cap` clips; a judgement against a limit is a `flag` |
| get / read / look up | fetch reference data | `read` and `look up` |
| fill / pad | replace a missing value | `fill`, with where (the ends) as an argument |
| field groups / column prefixes | the groups of @sec-field-groups and the prefixes of @sec-resolution-groups | one mapping: identification `vessel_`, temporal envelope `time_`, spatial envelope `place_`, configuration `gear_`, observation `catch_` |

Port and harbour stay as decided: "port" is the place word, and two ramb functions keep "harbour".

### Mirrors not yet needed

**decode** (a rectangle to its centre or bounds) and **thin** (down-sampling a track) are the mirrors of encode and
interpolate. Neither exists. The names are reserved here so that each pairs with its mirror when it comes.

# Scope

The grammar fixes the structure, the keys and the names. It does not fix the vocabularies: which gear codes, port
codes or species codes are valid. Those are lookup tables beside the grammar (gear, port and species references, the
ICES code lists), so the grammar stays stable while they change.

What is built today is the fishing side: trips, stations, fishing samples, catch, the track and the landings. Next are
the configuration and environment tables (plan 020). Survey hauls, casts and the sensor layer use the same shapes
when they come in, with `.smid` as soon as one station holds two samples.
